opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should push back on the premise a little. I don't work inside a frontier AI company. I run Redwood Research, which is a small independent nonprofit. We collaborate a lot with people at the labs, and we've done projects jointly with them, but we're outside. So I can tell you how it looks from my side of the fence, which is maybe the more interesting angle anyway.

There are real tradeoffs. Being outside gives you some things you can't easily get inside. We can say what we actually think about how much risk the companies are taking without running it past a comms team. We can work on things that might be awkward for a company, like threat models where the AI is actively scheming against its developers, which some people at labs find uncomfortable to put in an official document. And we can publish methods that any developer can pick up, rather than producing something tailored to one company's internal infrastructure.

The big cost is access and adoption. A lot of the most important safety work is now about how techniques interact with the real deployment setup: which models are monitored, what the agent scaffolds look like, what permissions the AI has, how the security team operates. From outside, you're often guessing. You write a paper saying, "Here's a protocol for catching a misaligned model that tries to sabotage your code," and then someone inside has to translate that into their actual system, with their actual latency and cost constraints. If no one inside champions it, it just sits there.

So the way we've tried to deal with that is to make our research as legible and cheap to adopt as possible, and to invest in relationships with the people at the labs who care about this stuff. A lot of the actual impact goes through those people. If a researcher at a lab reads our work and thinks it's sensible, they can push for it internally in a way I never could.

My overall take is that the ecosystem needs both. You want people inside who have the context and can actually change what gets deployed, and you want people outside who can set the research agenda somewhat independently, say uncomfortable things, and serve as a check. If everyone doing safety work were inside the companies, I think the field would end up quietly shaped by what's convenient for those companies, and that seems bad.

r001.rationale: The response describes limited outside access and the need for an internal champion to translate research into a lab’s deployment setup. It does not identify companies’ reluctance to adopt ideas originating elsewhere as a barrier to spreading research across companies.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that affiliation with a prominent frontier AI company, or that company’s reputation, makes other organizations more likely to adopt safety research.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts outside independence with inside access to deployment details, but does not state that the advantage of working inside a frontier AI company for adoption elsewhere depends on the kind of research.

fable-5.1.text:
So I should say up front: I'm not actually inside a frontier lab. Redwood is an independent nonprofit, and that's a deliberate choice, so I'm probably the wrong person to speak from the inside perspective. But I've thought about this question a lot, because it's basically the question of where Redwood should sit in the ecosystem.

The honest version is that being outside has costs and benefits, and the costs are real. People at labs have access to the frontier models, they have compute, they know what the actual deployment plans look like, and when they come up with a safety technique there's a direct path to it getting shipped. If you're at Anthropic and you build a control protocol, you can walk down the hall and talk to the people who'd implement it. We can't do that. We have to write it up, publish it, and hope people read it.

But I think the benefits of being outside are underrated, and they're mostly about credibility and about what you can say. When Redwood puts out a paper saying "here's a threat model we think labs should take seriously, and here's what adequate mitigation looks like," nobody has to wonder whether we're shading our conclusions to make our employer look good or to avoid implying our employer should spend a lot more money on safety. That matters a lot when you're talking to people at other labs, or to governments, or to the broader research community. If I were at one lab and I said "every lab should do this expensive thing," people at the other labs would reasonably hear that as partly a competitive move.

There's also a thing where lab researchers often can't talk about their most important work, or can only talk about it in sanitized form. We can be very concrete about threat models, about how we think models might try to subvert oversight, about what we think current practices get wrong. That concreteness is a big part of why the AI control agenda has gotten traction, I think. People can actually see what we're proposing.

And in practice the way we've tried to get adoption is by collaborating closely with people at labs while staying independent. A lot of our best work has been joint with researchers at Anthropic and elsewhere. We bring the research direction and the willingness to be blunt; they bring access and the ability to actually run things on real models at scale. I think that split has worked pretty well, and it's part of why I'm fairly bullish on there being a healthy independent safety research sector alongside the lab teams, rather than everyone being absorbed into the companies.

The thing I'd worry about, if I were inside, is less "will my research get adopted elsewhere" and more "will I notice when my organization's incentives are pulling my own judgment." That's a hard thing to monitor from inside, and it's one of the main reasons I've wanted Redwood to stay outside.

r001.rationale: The response says outside researchers must publish and hope others read their work, but it does not identify companies’ reluctance to adopt ideas because they originated elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It describes independent status as a source of credibility and says lab affiliation can make proposals seem competitive; it does not say a prominent company’s reputation makes other organizations more likely to adopt its research.

r003.rationale: The response discusses general tradeoffs of working inside or outside a lab, but does not state that the adoption advantage of working inside depends on the kind of research.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps a lot with getting your research adopted at the company you work at, but it doesn’t necessarily help nearly as much with getting it adopted elsewhere. A lot of adoption happens through fairly informal things: you know the people who would need to implement something, you understand what problems they’re actually facing, and you can keep talking to them as they try it out. Being inside the company is really useful for that.

But those advantages don’t automatically transfer to another company. And there can be disadvantages: you might not be able to share the details of what you did, or people at the other company might be less comfortable telling you about their systems. Whereas an independent safety organisation can potentially have relationships with several companies and be a more natural partner for all of them.

So I’d distinguish ‘Can I make this work in a real frontier AI system?’ from ‘Can I get lots of companies to use it?’ Working inside a lab seems particularly helpful for the first, and the second requires some additional story.

r001.rationale: It discusses weaker adoption at other companies and possible sharing or trust barriers, but does not identify reluctance to adopt ideas because they originated elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a prominent company’s reputation makes other organizations more likely to adopt its research.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes adoption inside a company from adoption across companies, but does not say the external-adoption advantage depends on the kind of research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a mixed bag. Working inside a frontier AI company gives you a much better sense of what problems actually arise and what kinds of interventions people would realistically use. You also have access to the models and infrastructure, and relationships with people who can put your research into practice. Those are pretty substantial advantages.

But getting something adopted at your company is different from getting it adopted elsewhere. Some of your work might be confidential, or depend on infrastructure that other companies don’t have. And people at another lab might reasonably wonder whether your results apply to their situation.

So I wouldn’t assume that being inside automatically gives you more influence across the industry. An independent organisation can sometimes be better placed to work with several companies and publish things that everyone can use. A lot depends on whether the particular research needs deep access to one company, or whether its value comes from being applicable across companies.

r001.rationale: The response mentions confidentiality and other labs questioning whether results apply to them, but does not identify reluctance to adopt ideas because they originated elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a prominent company’s reputation would make other organizations more likely to adopt its research.

r003.rationale: It says the advantage depends on whether the research needs deep access to one company or is valuable across companies.
